---
title: "Custom syntax highlighting via Lua filters"
---

Quarto's syntax-highlighting feature is driven by an attribute on the
AST: a `data-hl-spans` key on a `CodeBlock` (or inline `Code`) whose
value is a JSON array of `[start, end, capture]` triples. The
built-in pipeline stage produces this attribute from tree-sitter
queries; **any Lua filter that writes the same shape produces
identical output**. This page is a practical guide for that filter
path.

## Encoding

`data-hl-spans` is a JSON array. Each entry is a three-element array:

```json
[start_byte, end_byte, capture_name]
```

- `start_byte` / `end_byte` are 0-based, half-open. `code[start..end]`
  (in Rust/tree-sitter semantics) is the highlighted span.
- `capture_name` is a dotted identifier like `keyword`, `string`,
  `function.builtin`, or anything you invent. Dots become hyphens in
  the rendered HTML class name: `function.builtin` →
  `hl-function-builtin`.

Nesting is implicit: a span whose range encloses a shorter one nests
around it when rendered. Order spans by start offset; the writer is
otherwise lenient.

## Minimal example

This filter highlights the literal words `ERROR` and `WARN` in any
code block whose first class is `log`:

```lua
function CodeBlock(cb)
  if cb.attr.classes[1] ~= "log" then return nil end

  local spans = {}
  for _, row in ipairs({ { "ERROR", "error" }, { "WARN", "warning" } }) do
    local needle, capture = row[1], row[2]
    local init = 1
    while true do
      local s, e = cb.text:find(needle, init, true)
      if not s then break end
      spans[#spans + 1] = { s - 1, e, capture }
      init = e + 1
    end
  end
  table.sort(spans, function(a, b) return a[1] < b[1] end)

  cb.attr.attributes["data-hl-spans"] = pandoc.json.encode(spans)
  return cb
end
```

The only attribute mutation needed is:

```lua
cb.attr.attributes["data-hl-spans"] = pandoc.json.encode(spans)
```

This writes directly through to the block's `Attr` and persists on
the returned `CodeBlock`. `cb.attributes[k] = v` also works as a
shortcut (Pandoc-compatible).

## Styling

Capture names become HTML classes with `hl-` prefix and dots
converted to hyphens. In your CSS or SCSS:

```css
.hl-error   { color: #c0392b; font-weight: bold; }
.hl-warning { color: #d35400; }
```

The default Quarto highlight theme ships rules for a broad taxonomy
(keyword, string, comment, function, …). For custom capture names,
ship your own stylesheet alongside the filter.

## End-to-end examples

Two fixtures in the test corpus are maintained as canonical
copy-paste references:

- `crates/quarto/tests/smoke-all/highlighting/04-filter/` — the
  literal-word pattern from the snippet above.
- `crates/quarto/tests/smoke-all/highlighting/06-filter-severity/` —
  a structured systemd-log highlighter with multiple captures
  (`severity.err`, `severity.warning`, `timestamp`, …).

Both use the same idiomatic pattern:
`cb.attr.attributes["data-hl-spans"] = pandoc.json.encode(spans)`.

## When to use this vs a tree-sitter grammar

Use a filter when:

- The language has no tree-sitter grammar and writing one is overkill.
- You want highlights that aren't lexical (e.g. "flag all instances of
  `TODO`" or "color log lines by severity").
- You're prototyping: a filter is ~30 lines of Lua.

Use a tree-sitter grammar when:

- The language is complex and you want robust, nested captures from
  real parsing.
- You want Quarto's built-in theme mappings out of the box.
- You want your highlights to survive arbitrary user edits
  (grammars update spans when the text changes; filters run once).

The two paths coexist — the built-in stage skips any block that
already has `data-hl-spans`, so filter-authored spans take precedence.
